## Why use nested assessment?

The edge-selection level controls which connections enter a CPM. Choosing it
using the same assessment predictions that are reported as final performance
can make the performance estimate optimistic. With nested assessment, each
outer training set has its own inner folds for choosing a level. The selected
level is then fitted on that outer training set and evaluated on the held-out
outer fold. Outer predictions estimate the performance of the entire
level-selection procedure, not that of a single fixed level.

## Set up an example

The following synthetic data have one row per subject and one column per
connection. The nuisance variable is passed to `cpm()` rather than regressed
out beforehand.

```{r}
library(cpmr)

set.seed(2026)
n <- 80
conmat <- matrix(rnorm(n * 120), nrow = n)
covariates <- matrix(rnorm(n), ncol = 1)
behav <- rowMeans(conmat[, 1:10, drop = FALSE]) +
  0.5 * covariates[, 1] + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)

model_spec <- spec(
  selection = cpm_selection_cor(criterion = "p_value"),
  construction = cpm_construction_strength(standardize_edges = TRUE)
)
```

## Compare levels inside each outer fold

Supply at least two unique, finite candidate levels between 0 and 1 via
`selection_levels`. They use the criterion in `spec`: here they are p-value
cutoffs. For `"absolute"`, they are absolute-correlation cutoffs; for
`"proportion"`, they are per-sign proportions. The fixed `level` in the
selection specification is replaced by each candidate during tuning.

```{r}
set.seed(123)
tuned <- cpm(
  conmat = conmat,
  behav = behav,
  spec = model_spec,
  covariates = covariates,
  resamples = 5,
  selection_levels = c(0.001, 0.01, 0.05),
  selection_metric = "rmse",
  inner_resamples = 4,
  return_edges = "none"
)

tuned
```

For each outer fold, `cpm()` compares the candidates using mean inner-fold
RMSE and chooses the smallest mean. The mean is over valid fold scores, with
each contributing fold weighted equally. Set `selection_metric = "mae"` to use
mean MAE instead; RMSE is the default. Ties are resolved by the order of
`selection_levels`. The default separate-sign construction uses the `joint`
prediction stream for selection; `sign_mode = "net"` uses the `net` stream.

`resamples` controls the outer folds and can also accept a list of assessment
row indices. `inner_resamples` is the number of randomly generated inner folds
within each outer training set; its default is 5. Set the random seed before
`cpm()` to reproduce both generated outer folds and inner folds. With manual
outer folds, the seed still controls the inner folds.

## Inspect choices and outer performance

The tuning table has one row per candidate and outer fold. For example, inspect
the candidate scores in the first fold and then the choice in every fold:

```{r}
tuning <- tidy(tuned, component = "tuning")
tuning[tuning$outer_fold == 1, ]
tuning[tuning$selected, ]
```

`estimate` is the mean inner-fold error, `n_inner_folds` counts the valid
scores contributing to that mean, and `selected` marks the chosen candidate.
Selections can differ across outer folds. These inner scores are used for
selection, not as the final performance estimate.

```{r}
summary(tuned)
tidy(tuned, component = "metrics", level = "pooled")
head(tuned$predictions)
```

The summary and pooled metrics use the outer-fold predictions. Because this
example includes covariates, the observed outcomes and predictions are on the
fold-specific residualized outcome scale: nuisance regressions are fitted on
the relevant training split and applied to its assessment split.

## Practical considerations

- Covariate adjustment, edge standardization, edge screening, and model fitting
  are learned within each training split; outer assessment data do not select
  the level. Avoid preprocessing the full dataset before calling `cpm()`.
- Candidate values of 0 or 1 produce a warning because selection may become
  degenerate. Choose candidates in advance and report the criterion, metric,
  outer and inner fold counts, seed, and covariate handling.
- Nested tuning evaluates the procedure; it does not return one final
  full-data model or identify a universally best level. Inspecting outer
  results to choose settings and reporting those same results as final
  performance would reuse assessment data for selection.
- Every outer training set must support the requested inner folds and their
  training requirements, including residual degrees of freedom when using
  covariates and p-value screening.
- Nested tuning is more expensive than a fixed-level run. Association
  statistics are reused across candidates within an inner split, but not
  across folds or calls. `return_edges = "none"` avoids storing edge masks.

See [Leakage-Safe Covariate Handling in CPM](anti-leakage-covariates.html) for
more on covariate handling and [Native Getting Started with
cpmr](native-getting-started.html) for the basic workflow.
